hook: Head office says 40% of customers buy a pastry with their coffee. At one store, only 105 of 300 sampled orders include one: 35%. Is that store really different, or would a gap that size show up by luck at a store that matches head office? The p-value puts a number on "by luck".

prereq.q: A study tests $H_0: p = 0.40$. Which large counts check is right for $n = 300$?
options: 300 is less than 10% of the population
prereq.why: A test checks large counts with the null value $p_0 = 0.40$, because it assumes $H_0$ is true.

prereq.q: For a normal distribution with mean 0.40 and standard deviation 0.0283, about what is the z-score of 0.35?
prereq.why: $z = \frac{0.35 - 0.40}{0.0283} = -1.77$: value minus mean, over the standard deviation.

figure.caption: A p-value is a tail area of the null distribution: one tail for a one-sided alternative, both tails for a two-sided one.

chain.effect: $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal with mean $p_0$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}$
the test statistic $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}$ says how many standard deviations it is from $p_0$

chain.cause: Find the area beyond $z$ in the direction of $H_a$ (both tails if two-sided)
chain.effect: that area is the p-value: the chance of a result at least this extreme if $H_0$ is true
the result would be rare under $H_0$, which is evidence against $H_0$ and for $H_a$ (but never proof)

ideas: Test statistic: $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}$, with $p_0$ in the square root.
p-value: the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed, in the direction of $H_a$. Two-sided: double one tail.
Interpret: "Assuming the true proportion of all __ is $p_0$, there is a __ probability of getting a sample proportion of __ or less (more) by chance in a random sample of __."
A simulation estimates a p-value: the share of simulated results, made assuming $H_0$, at least as extreme as the real one.
Not the probability that $H_0$ is true. A large p-value does not prove $H_0$.

misconception.wrong: A p-value of 0.0385 means there is a 3.85% chance that the null hypothesis is true.
misconception.right: The p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true. It is the probability of data at least this extreme if $H_0$ holds, not the probability that $H_0$ holds.

summary: A p-value measures how surprising the data are if $H_0$ is true. Assuming $H_0$ is true, standardize the sample proportion with $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}$ and find the tail area in the direction of $H_a$ (both tails for $\ne$). That area is the p-value: the chance of a result at least as extreme as the one observed if $H_0$ is true. Small p-values are evidence against $H_0$; they are never the probability that $H_0$ is true.
